<margin>Su's Commentary <note>Su Che (1039–1112), a prominent Song dynasty scholar and statesman</note></margin> When one does not yet understand the Dao and diligently pursues learning, hearing and seeing increase daily. Yet if one possesses no unifying principle to integrate them, this inevitably becomes a burdensome entanglement. Confucius said: "Hear much, select what is good and follow it; see much and commit it to memory. This is the second tier of knowing." If one day a person comes to understand the Dao, examining all former contrivance and artifice, not a single part will fail to appear false. Casting away delusion to recover one's true nature: this is called decrease. Confucius asked Zigong: "Do you consider me to be one who learns broadly and memorizes it all?" Zigong replied: "Indeed, is it not so?" Confucius answered: "No, I link it all with a single thread." When one forgets the calculating mind to recover pure nature, this may be termed decrease; yet if delusions still linger, one must go further, forgetting this very mind until the recovery of pure nature is complete without remainder. Only then does one shed deliberate striving without straying from <term>wuwei</term> <gloss>non-action, or effortless alignment with nature</gloss>. Common people all possess desire to govern the world and manage affairs; thus they invent projects and seek results, their intentions visibly projected outward. Others resent and recoil from this, making success difficult and out of reach. The sage practices <term>wuwei</term> and therefore creates no entanglement in affairs; his heart is made manifest without artifice, and all things find peace in him. Although he does not aggressively grasp the world's affairs to manipulate them, the affairs of the world accord and settle into peace thereby.

<margin>Lü's Commentary <note>Lü Huiqing (1032–1111), Northern Song scholar known for his Taoist commentaries</note></margin> The practitioner of learning is one who has not yet heard the Dao. Having not yet heard the Dao, in seeking it he must inevitably be broad; therefore it is said, "he increases." The practitioner of the Dao is one who has already heard the Dao. Having already heard the Dao, in practicing it he must inevitably abide in non-action alone; therefore it is said, "he decreases." To decrease and decrease again still falls short of escaping conscious action. Only when one decreases even the very act of decreasing does one at last arrive at <term>wuwei</term>. Non-action means absolute stillness without movement. Having nothing left undone means being stirred and thereupon penetrating all phenomena of the world. Moving through non-action to reach ultimate non-action is what is called the constant standard. To learn without anxiety is called divine; the working of the divine is the Dao itself. When it comes to the utmost divine, who can truly share in this? Viewed from this perspective, gaining the world is always accomplished through non-action; when one relies on purposeful striving, it is readily apparent that this is insufficient to gain the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai's Commentary <note>Song dynasty scholar</note></margin> Only after there is nothing one does not know can one speak of learning; therefore, in learning one desires daily increase. Only after there is nothing one does not accomplish can one speak of the Dao; therefore, in the Dao one desires daily decrease. Yet while increase can be pursued through gradual progress, decrease is difficult to attain by sheer force of will. Only those of consummate illumination can suddenly shed all attachments in an instant, arriving at the realm of <term>wuwei</term>. Thus they leave nothing undone; their applications are inexhaustible, and when extended to the world, they remain abundant and free.

<margin>Xizhai's Commentary <note>Lin Xiyi (ca. 1193–ca. 1271), Song dynasty scholar whose art name was Xizhai</note></margin> The pursuit of learning is meant for seeking knowledge, hence it increases daily. The pursuit of the Dao is meant for dispelling delusion, hence it decreases daily. If knowledge does not reach its utmost limit, decrease cannot be complete; therefore, daily increase serves as the foundation for daily decrease. If one decreases and decreases again, delusion vanishing and the true remaining whole, one attains <term>wuwei</term>. Once one arrives at non-action, then wherever purposeful action arises, it is never separate from non-action; this state cannot be simply characterized in terms of increase and decrease. When non-action reaches its culmination, though the affairs of the world be myriad, a single thread runs through them all. If one instead stirs up troubles out of a desire to manage affairs, one will hardly have leisure: a single matter before oneself will already be tangled and confused, so how much worse when facing the multitude of worldly affairs?

The sage has no fixed heart-mind; he takes the heart-mind of the common people as his own. Those who are good, I treat as good; those who are not good, I also treat as good, and thus virtue attains goodness. Those who are trustworthy, I trust; those who are not trustworthy, I also trust, and thus virtue attains trust. The sage dwells in the world with an unassuming, quiet mind; for the sake of the world, he unifies and harmonizes its heart. The common people all fasten their ears and eyes upon him, and the sage...

Laozi said: "As for men of clever knowledge and divine sagehood, I consider myself free of them. # Xunzi: Correct Discourse

In ancient times, the Son of Heaven commanded one thousand civil officers, and the feudal lords commanded one hundred civil officers. When, through these thousand officers, orders are executed throughout all the states of the Xia <note>meaning the civilized Chinese realm</note>, such a ruler is called a King. When, through these hundred officers, orders are executed throughout the borders of one's own territory, so that even though the state may suffer instability, it does not reach the point of collapse, usurpation, or ultimate ruin <gloss>the character for ruin is read as collapse, meaning the downfall of one's inherited rule</gloss>, such a ruler is called a True Prince. 

Consider the successor of a sage king: he inherits possession of the realm, holds custody of the governing records and registers, and stands at the head of the ancestral lineage of All under Heaven. Yet if he lacks talent and fails to attain upright virtue <gloss>failing to attain uprightness</gloss>, internally the common people will detest him, and externally the feudal lords will rebel against him. Close at hand, authority within his own borders will dissolve; far afield, the feudal lords will refuse obedience. His commands will not be obeyed even within his own territory. In worse cases, feudal lords will encroach upon his territory, diminish his lands, and launch punitive military campaigns against him. When circumstances reach this point, then even if he has not yet perished outright, I say that he no longer possesses All under Heaven.

When the sage king has died, and those holding custody of the governing registers are feeble and incapable <gloss>slack, weak, and unfit for the responsibilities of office</gloss>, insufficient to bind together <gloss>hang together or maintain</gloss> All under Heaven, then All under Heaven is left without a true ruler. If among the feudal lords there arises one whose virtue is brilliant, whose awe-inspiring power accumulates, and whom none among the people within the four seas do not desire to take as their lord and master; and if, when an aggressive state behaves with isolated arrogance <gloss>referring to oppressive tyrants like Jie and Zhou acting with wanton license</gloss>, he then executes punitive retribution upon it <gloss>in this context, acting upon necessity</gloss>; and if he is sure not to harm innocent people, putting to death the tyrant ruler as easily as executing a lone scoundrel forsaken by all <gloss>a tyrant abandoned by All under Heaven, standing entirely isolated as a single lone man</gloss>: if he is like this, he may truly be said to know how to govern All under Heaven. 

To be capable of governing All under Heaven is what is called being a true King. Tang and Wu did not seize All under Heaven by force. They cultivated their moral Way, practiced their righteousness, shared common benefits with All under Heaven, and eliminated common harms for All under Heaven, so that All under Heaven willingly flocked to them. Jie and Zhou did not have All under Heaven stripped from them by others. They inverted the virtues of Yu and Tang, disrupted the social distinctions of ritual and righteousness, acted like beasts, accumulated misfortunes, and brought ruin upon themselves <gloss>meaning that All under Heaven abandoned them of their own accord</gloss>.

<summary>Xunzi defines kingship and rulership through moral efficacy and legitimate command rather than inherited privilege, arguing that tyrants like Jie and Zhou naturally forfeited the realm while sage kings Tang and Wu received it through shared benefit and justice.</summary>

Section 3: Revealing the characteristics of the conditioned arising above. This refers to the sentence regarding the "defiled mind."

First, the heading:
There are six kinds of defiled mind.

Second, the inquiry:
What are the six?
Within each of the six there are two parts: first the obstruction, and second the remedy.

Third, the explanation:
Now, these six defilements correspond in reverse order to the first four among the six coarse marks and the three subtle marks following them. Due to the <term>Treatise on Awakening of Faith Commentary</term> <gloss>Qi xin lun shu</gloss>, Fascicle 1, same as above: this first stage combines the third and fourth among those coarse marks, therefore there are only six. Thus, these names are borrowed to outline these six.

First, the marks of grasping and reckoning with names:

The first is the defilement corresponding to attachment. Because it is distanced and left behind by relying on the liberation of the two vehicles and the stage corresponding to faith. This is the third and fourth marks among the six coarse marks. It is also the meaning of what is nourished by the afflictions of view and love of the mental consciousness mentioned above. It is also the mark of discriminating and attaching to places among the four marks above. However, the coarse mind externally grasps and corresponds with objects, defiling its pure practice, hence it is termed "defilement." When the liberation of the two vehicles reaches the stage of no-more-learning, the afflictions of view and cultivation are completely abandoned. Those "corresponding to faith" refers to those from the ten understandings onward whose root of faith is perfected without regression, termed "corresponding to faith." Therefore, the <term>Treatise on the Ten Stages</term> <gloss>Daśabhūmika-śāstra</gloss> states: "Prior to the stages, it is collectively termed the stage of faith practice for bodhisattvas." Asanga's treatise also agrees with this statement. This bodhisattva

<column-break/>

attains the emptiness of person, so the afflictions of view and cultivation cannot arise actively, hence it is said to be "distanced and left behind." It is not said in terms of dormant tendencies, because afflictions are retained intentionally. The <term>Summary of the Great Vehicle</term> <gloss>Mahāyānasaṃgraha</gloss> states: "If one does not sever the active mind, one is no different from ordinary beings; if one does not retain the seeds of affliction, one is no different from the two vehicles." Furthermore, there are two intentions in retaining afflictions: for oneself and for others. This is explained according to the Final Teaching. If explained according to the Initial Teaching, retaining afflictions is only spoken of from the first stage onward, as explained in other treatises. Now, this bodhisattva not only severs the grasping to a personal self of the four dwelling states, but also partially severs the dwelling stage of ignorance. Therefore, later in this treatise it states: "Those who do not comprehend the meaning of the single Dharma-realm observe and train in severing it from the stage corresponding to faith onward." Thus, this is only to reveal the coarseness of personal selfhood, so that aspect is not discussed here.

Second, the continuous mark:

The second is the uninterrupted corresponding defilement. Because by relying on the stage corresponding to faith, practicing skillful means, one is gradually able to abandon it, and upon attaining the stage of a pure mind, one is completely free from it.
<term>Treatise on Awakening of Faith Commentary</term> <gloss>Qi xin lun shu</gloss>, Fascicle 1, same as above.
This is the second among the six coarse marks. From this up to the sixth, it again corresponds in reverse to the previous five consciousnesses, this position being the fifth. Simply grasping dharmas with continuous generation, arising without interruption, that is precisely the meaning of "continuity." From the ten understandings onward, through the skillful means of consciousness-only contemplation, investigation, and reflection, up to the first stage where one realizes the three non-natures and all-pervading true suchness, the discrimination of grasping to dharmas cannot arise actively.
